images.alt: The Taj Mahal seen in the distance across the Yamuna from a domed pavilion of Agra Fort
images.caption: The Taj Mahal from Agra Fort

overview.text:
Agra, on the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh, is the city of the Taj Mahal — and it holds two more World Heritage Sites besides: the red sandstone Agra Fort and, 37 km away, Akbar's abandoned capital of Fatehpur Sikri. Smaller Mughal monuments fill the gaps, from the inlaid tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah to the riverside garden of Mehtab Bagh, which looks straight across the water at the Taj.

Most visitors give Agra one or two days. The single most important thing to plan around is Friday: the Taj Mahal is closed that day, while Agra's other monuments open daily from sunrise to sunset. The official tourism site recommends October to March as the best season; summers are hot and dry, and winter fog can delay morning trains.

The guides below cover each monument's visiting rules, fees and best times, followed by how to get here from Delhi, where to stay, what to eat and a ready-made two-day plan.

items.body: Taj Mahal at sunrise: Arrive for the 30-minutes-before-sunrise opening for softer light and smaller crowds than at sunset.
Agra Fort: Akbar's red sandstone fortress with Shah Jahan's marble pavilions and views of the Taj.
Fatehpur Sikri: Akbar's capital from 1571 to 1585, a day trip 37 km from the city.
The 'Baby Taj': I'timad-ud-Daulah's tomb, a jewel box of marble inlay that predates the Taj.
Mehtab Bagh at sunset: The garden across the river, aligned with the Taj — open on Fridays too.

best_time.text:
The official Taj Mahal website names October to March as the best season. Agra's summers are hot and dry and the monsoon brings rain; in mid-winter, fog across the plains often delays early trains, so leave slack in your plans if you are arriving by rail in December or January.

Whatever the month, go early: the official site notes that early mornings avoid both the summer heat and the crowds, and that sunset tends to be busier than sunrise. Remember the Taj is closed every Friday — use that day for Fatehpur Sikri or Mehtab Bagh.

how_to_reach.text:
By road, Agra is about 204 km from Delhi and 232 km from Jaipur. The 165.5 km Yamuna Expressway runs from Greater Noida, on Delhi's edge, to Agra. Delhi's international airport, about 200 km away, is the usual gateway for international visitors; Agra's own airport at Kheria is a small domestic civil enclave on an Air Force base.

By train, Agra Cantonment is the main station, with Raja-ki-Mandi and Agra Fort stations also serving the city. The main trains from Delhi include the Shatabdi, Rajdhani, Gatimaan and Taj Express; note that the Gatimaan Express does not run on Fridays — the same day the Taj Mahal is closed. Check current timings and fares on IRCTC before you book.

local_transport.text:
Taxis, auto-rickshaws and cycle-rickshaws are easy to find, and prepaid taxis can be hired for trips to nearby places such as Fatehpur Sikri. The Agra Metro opened in March 2024; its Yellow Line runs between Sikandra and the Taj East Gate.

Petrol and diesel vehicles cannot go within 500 m of the Taj Mahal. Park at Shilpgram for the east gate or Amrood ka Teela for the west gate, then take a battery bus or golf cart to the entrance.

where_to_stay.text:
Staying close to the Taj Mahal makes the sunrise opening much easier. The lanes around the east and west gates have guesthouses and smaller hotels within walking distance or a short ride; larger hotels are spread further out along the main roads, a short taxi or auto-rickshaw ride away.

Whichever area you choose, check how your hotel will get you to the gate before dawn — vehicles are stopped 500 m from the Taj, so the last stretch is on foot, by battery bus or by golf cart.

items.body: Mughlai dishes — Agra is known for this rich, slow-cooked cuisine.
Petha, Agra's best-known sweet, made from ash gourd and sold in many varieties.
Bedai with jalebi, a popular local breakfast.
Bhalla (dahi aloo tikki) from the Sadar Bazaar area, and tandoori chai served in clay cups.
Inside the Taj Mahal, keep your phone silent and your voice low — the mausoleum is a tomb.
Photography is not allowed inside the main mausoleum; take pictures outside instead.
At Fatehpur Sikri's Jama Masjid and the tomb of Salim Chishti, dress modestly and follow any requests to remove shoes or cover your head.
Don't touch or scratch the marble and inlay — these are fragile heritage surfaces.

items.title: Visas
items.body: Apply for an e-Tourist visa at least 4 days before you arrive; your passport needs at least six months' validity.

items.title: Payments
items.body: International visitors can pay by scanning QR codes using NPCI's UPI One World wallet, set up after a passport-and-visa KYC check at airports, hotels or money changers. Keep some cash for small purchases.

items.title: Monument tickets
items.body: Buy online through the ASI to save a little and skip the window queue; children under 15 enter free.

items.title: What to carry
items.body: Travel light for the Taj: food, tripods, chargers, headphones and large bags are refused at security.

items.title: Emergency
items.body: Call 112 for the police and emergency services in Uttar Pradesh.

items.title: Guides and touts
items.body: Hire only approved guides and photographers who can show their identity cards.

items.title: Heat
items.body: In summer, sightsee early, carry water and rest indoors in the middle of the day.

items.title: Getting around safely
items.body: Agree the fare before an auto-rickshaw ride, or use prepaid taxis.

items.title: Which day is the Taj Mahal closed?
items.body: Every Friday. All other days it opens from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes before sunset.

items.title: How many days do I need in Agra?
items.body: One full day covers the Taj Mahal, Agra Fort and the Baby Taj; add a second day for Fatehpur Sikri and Mehtab Bagh at sunset.

items.title: Can I see the Taj Mahal on a Friday?
items.body: Not from inside, but Mehtab Bagh across the river gives a full view of it on Fridays.

items.title: Can I visit the Taj Mahal at night?
items.body: Yes, on five nights around each full moon, in small timed batches. Tickets are sold by the Archaeological Survey of India in advance, not at the gate on the night — check the current booking process with the ASI.
Plan your Friday around the Taj Mahal's weekly closure — Fatehpur Sikri and Mehtab Bagh are both open.
Buy monument tickets online in advance to avoid queues at the windows.
Leave food, tripods and chargers at your hotel before visiting the Taj.

overview.text:
The Taj Mahal was commissioned by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in 1631 in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Work began the following year; the white marble mausoleum was finished in 1648 and the surrounding buildings and gardens five years later. It stands on the right bank of the Yamuna in Agra, framed by red sandstone gateways, mosques and a formal garden, and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

It is India's most visited ticketed monument: in 2024–25 it drew 6.26 million domestic and 0.65 million foreign visitors. That popularity shapes the visit. Come at the opening, 30 minutes before sunrise, when the official site says both the heat and the crowds are lighter, and remember the monument is closed every Friday.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes before sunset. Closed on Fridays.

items.title: Entry fee (foreign visitors)
items.body: ₹1,100, plus ₹200 (optional) to enter the main mausoleum. Includes ASI and ADA fees.

items.title: Entry fee (Indian visitors)
items.body: ₹50, plus ₹200 (optional) for the main mausoleum.

items.title: SAARC and BIMSTEC citizens
items.body: ₹540, plus ₹200 (optional) for the main mausoleum.

items.title: Children
items.body: Free for children under 15.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: At the ticket windows at the gates, or online through the Archaeological Survey of India (online tickets are ₹5 cheaper for Indians and ₹50 for foreigners).

items.title: Gates
items.body: Enter by the east or west gate; the southern gate is currently closed for entry.

items.title: Night viewing
items.body: Five nights a month around the full moon, 20:00–23:59, in half-hour batches of up to 50 people. ₹750 for foreigners, ₹510 for Indian visitors. Buy in advance from the ASI.

items.title: Taj Museum
items.body: Inside the complex; 10 am–5 pm, free.
Leave food, tobacco, chargers, headphones and tripods behind — they are refused at security, and drones are banned.
Photography is fine in the gardens but not inside the main mausoleum.
Vehicles stop 500 m away; battery buses and golf carts run from the car parks to the gates (included for foreign visitors, ₹25 for Indians).
Hire only approved guides who can show an ID card.

overview.text:
Agra Fort was rebuilt in red sandstone by the emperor Akbar between 1565 and 1573 and remained the main residence of the Mughal rulers until 1638, when the capital moved to Delhi. Akbar's grandson Shah Jahan later added white marble buildings — the Diwan-i-Am, Diwan-i-Khas, Khas Mahal, Moti Masjid and the Musamman Burj, where Shah Jahan died in 1666.

The fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1983, and lies about 2.5 km north-west of the Taj Mahal. From the balconies of its riverside pavilions you look across the Yamuna to the Taj, which makes it a good pairing on the same day. Plan on about two hours inside; part of the fort is still used by the Indian Army and is closed to visitors.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset, every day.

items.title: Entry fee
items.body: Foreign visitors ₹650 (₹600 on Fridays); Indian visitors ₹50 (₹40 on Fridays). Children under 15 free.

items.title: Entrance
items.body: Through the Amar Singh Gate only.

items.title: Getting there
items.body: About 5.5 km from Agra Cantt railway station and 2.5 km from the Taj Mahal.
Visit after an early Taj Mahal visit, then look back at the Taj from the riverside pavilions.
Wear comfortable shoes — the courtyards and ramps are extensive.

places.name: Fatehpur Sikri
places.summary: Akbar's red sandstone capital from 1571 to 1585, now a World Heritage Site and the classic day trip from Agra.
places.seoTitle: Fatehpur Sikri Day Trip from Agra: Guide & Tickets
places.seoDescription: Plan a day trip to Fatehpur Sikri, 37 km from Agra: Akbar's palaces, the Buland Darwaza, the tomb of Salim Chishti, entry fees and tips.

images.alt: The red sandstone Diwan-i-Khas with rooftop kiosks in the palace courtyard of Fatehpur Sikri
images.caption: Diwan-i-Khas, Fatehpur Sikri

overview.text:
Akbar founded Fatehpur Sikri as the capital of the Mughal Empire in 1571, and it served in that role until 1585. Built in red sandstone about 37 km from Agra, the city was abandoned not long after, which is why its palaces, courtyards and mosque survive so completely. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

The visit falls into two parts. The palace complex begins at the Diwan-i-Am, the Hall of Public Audience, and includes the Diwan-i-Khas, whose single chamber is built around a carved central column. Next door, the Jama Masjid is entered through the towering Buland Darwaza, built to mark Akbar's campaign in Gujarat; in its courtyard stands the white marble tomb of the Sufi saint Salim Chishti. Allow two to three hours on site.

items.title: Entry fee
items.body: The official fee table lists ₹610 for foreign visitors (₹600 on Fridays or after visiting the Taj) and ₹50 for Indian visitors (₹40 on Fridays). Children under 15 free.

items.title: Getting there
items.body: About 37 km from Agra by road — hire a prepaid taxi for the round trip.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Check current timings with the Archaeological Survey of India before you go.
Go on a Friday, when the Taj Mahal is closed.
Dress modestly for the Jama Masjid and the saint's tomb, which are active places of worship.

places.name: Tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah
places.summary: The 'Baby Taj': a small marble tomb covered in inlay, built by Nur Jahan for her father between 1622 and 1628.
places.seoDescription: Visit the Tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah, Agra's 'Baby Taj': history, the marble inlay that inspired the Taj Mahal, entry fees and when to go.

images.alt: Front view of the marble Tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah with its four corner towers
images.caption: The 'Baby Taj'

images.alt: Corner tower and inlaid marble walls of the Tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah
images.caption: Inlaid marble walls

overview.text:
Built between 1622 and 1628, this tomb was commissioned by the empress Nur Jahan for her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, who held the title I'timad-ud-Daulah. It is popularly called the 'Baby Taj', and the name fits: although small, it marks the turning point in Mughal architecture from red sandstone to the white marble and pietra dura inlay that reached its height at the Taj Mahal.

The tomb sits on the east bank of the Yamuna, in a quiet walled garden that sees far fewer visitors than the Taj. Look closely at the walls — almost every surface is inlaid with coloured stone patterns of flowers, vessels and geometric designs. An hour is enough, and it combines well with Mehtab Bagh later in the afternoon.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset, every day (like Agra's other monuments apart from the Taj).

items.title: Entry fee
items.body: The official fee table lists ₹310 for foreign visitors (₹300 on Fridays or after visiting the Taj) and ₹30 for Indian visitors (₹25 on Fridays). Children under 15 free.
Visit in the late afternoon, when the marble glows and the garden is calm.
Combine it with Mehtab Bagh on the same side of the river.

places.name: Mehtab Bagh
places.summary: A Mughal garden across the Yamuna, aligned with the Taj Mahal — the place to see the Taj at sunset, and on Fridays.
places.seoTitle: Mehtab Bagh: Taj Mahal Sunset View Point, Agra
places.seoDescription: Visit Mehtab Bagh, the Mughal garden aligned with the Taj Mahal across the Yamuna: the best sunset and Friday view of the Taj, entry and seasonal tips.

images.commons: File:View of Taj Mahal from Mehtab Bagh gardens.jpg
images.alt: The Taj Mahal seen at the end of a long lawn and hedges in the Mehtab Bagh garden
images.caption: The Taj Mahal from Mehtab Bagh

overview.text:
Mehtab Bagh is a square Mughal garden on the north bank of the Yamuna, directly opposite the Taj Mahal and aligned with it. Today it is the best place to see the Taj from across the river — and because it stays open on Fridays, it is also the only way to see the monument when the Taj itself is closed.

The garden is low-key: lawns, hedges and pathways leading to the riverbank, with the Taj filling the view across the water. Come in the late afternoon and stay for sunset. In the monsoon parts of the garden can flood, so check conditions after heavy rain.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset; confirm evening hours locally, as the official pages differ.

items.title: Entry fee
items.body: Official pages list ₹200–₹300 for foreign visitors and ₹25–₹50 for Indian visitors; confirm at the ticket window.

items.title: Fridays
items.body: Open — a good way to see the Taj Mahal on the day it is closed.
Arrive an hour before sunset for the best light on the Taj.
In the monsoon, check that the garden isn't waterlogged before heading over.

itineraries.title: Two days in Agra: the Taj, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri
itineraries.summary: An unhurried two-day plan: the Taj Mahal at sunrise, Agra Fort and the Baby Taj, then a day trip to Fatehpur Sikri and sunset at Mehtab Bagh.
itineraries.seoTitle: 2 Days in Agra Itinerary: Taj Mahal & Fatehpur Sikri
itineraries.seoDescription: A realistic two-day Agra itinerary: Taj Mahal at sunrise, Agra Fort, the Baby Taj, Fatehpur Sikri and Mehtab Bagh, with timings, entry fees and Friday tips.

plan.overview: Two full days cover Agra's three World Heritage Sites without rushing. The plan starts each day early to beat the heat and the crowds and keeps the hottest hours free for lunch and rest. It assumes you arrive the evening before; if one of your days is a Friday, make that Day 2 — the Taj Mahal is closed on Fridays, but Fatehpur Sikri and Mehtab Bagh are open.

days.title: The Taj Mahal and Agra Fort
days.summary: Mughal Agra's two great monuments, with a quiet afternoon at the Baby Taj.

stops.name: Taj Mahal
stops.note: Gates open 30 minutes before sunrise. Allow time for security; enter the main mausoleum with the optional ₹200 ticket.

stops.name: Agra Fort
stops.note: Enter by the Amar Singh Gate; look for the Taj from the riverside pavilions.

stops.name: Lunch and a break from the heat

days.travel: Short taxi or auto-rickshaw rides: the fort is about 2.5 km from the Taj, and the Baby Taj is across the river (estimate: 15–30 minutes per hop, depending on traffic).
days.meals: Breakfast after the Taj; lunch near Agra Fort or back at your hotel; try petha or bedai with jalebi.

days.title: Fatehpur Sikri and Mehtab Bagh
days.summary: Akbar's abandoned capital, then the Taj at sunset from across the Yamuna.

stops.name: Drive to Fatehpur Sikri
stops.duration: About 1–1.5 hours each way (estimate for 37 km)

stops.name: Fatehpur Sikri
stops.note: Palace complex first, then the Jama Masjid through the Buland Darwaza and the tomb of Salim Chishti.

stops.name: Mehtab Bagh
stops.note: Stay for sunset over the Taj Mahal.

days.travel: A prepaid taxi for the Fatehpur Sikri round trip is the simplest option.
days.meals: Carry water and snacks for the morning; lunch back in Agra.
days.overnight: Agra, or travel on by evening train

budget.assumptions: Entry fees per adult foreign visitor, from the official Agra monument fee table. Children under 15 enter free. Accommodation, transport and meals vary too widely to estimate here.

booking.detail: Buy online through the ASI (cheaper) or at the gates.
Only on five nights around the full moon; tickets are sold in advance by the ASI — check the current booking process.
Book Delhi–Agra trains on IRCTC; the Gatimaan Express doesn't run on Fridays.

alternatives: Short on time? Do Day 1 only, and see Mehtab Bagh at sunset instead of the Baby Taj.
If your visit falls on a full-moon week, add a night viewing of the Taj on Day 1.
Prefer to skip the drive? Replace Fatehpur Sikri with a slower morning at Agra Fort and the Taj Museum.
tips: Leave food, tripods and chargers at the hotel on Taj day.
Hire only approved guides who can show an ID card.
